1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks the extra pawn on e4, so Black has to decide at once how to hold it. White commits to a gambit: a pawn down in return for quick development and open lines, and Black's task is to survive the early initiative and keep the material.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Be3.strategy: Guards d4 and develops, but does not attack the pawn on e4, so there is no pressure on it yet. A quieter way into the gambit that leaves White a free hand over the set-up, though Black gets time to organise the defence of the extra pawn.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Be3.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Diemer-Rosenberg Attack

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops with an eye on f7, but the bishop does nothing about the extra pawn on e4. Black keeps it and develops freely, while White has created neither the pawn lever nor the piece pressure that make a gambit worth its price.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Bc4.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Fritz Attack

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.f3.strategy: Attacks e4 with the pawn before any piece is out, which takes f3 from the king's knight and weakens the e1-h4 diagonal. Black strikes back with ...e5: if White takes on e5, the queen trade costs the right to castle, and if White takes on e4, ...exd4 leaves Black a pawn up.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.f3.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Blackmar Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.f3.background: Its popularity was short-lived, since the gambit was basically unsound: Black secures a superior position with 3...e5.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: The natural defence: the knight guards the pawn on e4 and develops towards the centre. Black accepts the gambit and keeps the extra pawn for now, while White gets a lead in development and the chance to open the f-file; Black must neutralise that initiative before the pawn counts.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: Strikes at the d4 pawn instead of guarding e4. If White takes on e5, the queens come off and White either loses the right to castle or has to undevelop the knight, so the game heads for a quiet, equal endgame. Black trades the gambit's sting for safety.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Bf5.strategy: Defends the pawn with the bishop and brings it out before ...e6 can shut it in. The pawn on e4 cramps White, since a knight arriving on f3 or a bishop on d3 would be taken by it. White usually attacks the pawn a second time with the f-pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 f5.strategy: Holds the pawn with the f-pawn, but at a price: the e8-h5 diagonal opens, so the white queen can give check on h5, and the kingside is loosened while Black's pieces are still at home. White can first prevent ...e5 and then attack e4 again.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 f5.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Netherlands Variation
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 f5.background: The name comes from the Dutch Defence, which can also reach this position through 1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 d5 3.e4 dxe4.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once instead of defending the extra pawn. White can push d5 to gain space and keep the knight's pressure on e4, so Black's counterattack soon needs more support than it has. A rarely tested countergambit that leaves Black short of development.
1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4 3.Nc3 c5.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit: Reversed Albin Countergambit
